entries.title: Transcription
entries.summary: Make an RNA copy of a stretch of DNA. The DNA stays in place while the cell builds a new RNA strand.
entries.explanation: For a human protein-coding gene, RNA polymerase II reads one DNA strand—the template—and joins RNA building blocks in a matching order. Other proteins help the machinery get started and keep it working.
entries.playfulAside: A working copy, not a DNA moving day.
entries.deeperDetail: The template is read 3′ → 5′, while RNA grows 5′ → 3′. New building blocks attach to the RNA’s 3′ end. Some RNA processing can begin while transcription is still happening.
entries.simplification: This overview leaves out many regulatory proteins and molecular steps. It does not describe every type of transcription.

evidence.statement: Polymerase II catalyzes DNA-directed RNA synthesis.
Transcription includes initiation, elongation, and termination.
Elongation involves additional factors and can be coupled to RNA processing.
The template strand is read 3′ → 5′ while RNA grows 5′ → 3′.
The growing RNA 3′ end engages the polymerase active site.
New RNA building blocks attach to the growing RNA’s 3′ end.
The template DNA stays in place while a matching RNA strand is built.
RNA building blocks match the template strand in complementary order.
Other proteins help the transcription machinery get started and continue working.
RNA polymerase II transcribes human protein-coding genes in the nucleus.

entries.title: Nucleus
entries.summary: A membrane-enclosed compartment that holds most of a human cell’s DNA.
entries.explanation: In a human cell that has a nucleus, nuclear genes are transcribed here. RNA transcripts are also processed here, and nuclear pores help control what moves in and out.
entries.playfulAside: Important documents inside. Controlled traffic at the doors.
entries.deeperDetail: The nuclear envelope surrounds the nucleus. The fluid interior is called the nucleoplasm. Not every human cell has a nucleus—for example, mature red blood cells do not.
entries.simplification: The document-storage comparison is a memory aid, not a literal description of how DNA works.

evidence.statement: The nucleus holds most of a human cell’s DNA inside a surrounding membrane.
Nuclear genes are transcribed and their RNA transcripts processed in the nucleus.
Nuclear pores help control movement into and out of the nucleus.
Mature human red blood cells do not have a nucleus.

entries.title: RNA polymerase II
entries.summary: A molecular machine that builds RNA using DNA as a template.
entries.explanation: Polymerase II links RNA building blocks into a growing strand. It works with other proteins, so it is not a one-molecule construction crew.
entries.playfulAside: RNA assembly crew: now hiring matching building blocks.
entries.deeperDetail: Its active site is the region where RNA building blocks are joined. During elongation, the growing RNA’s 3′ end sits at this site. The incoming building blocks are ribonucleoside triphosphates: ATP, UTP, CTP, and GTP.
entries.simplification: A cartoon character represents a protein complex. Its face and personality are decorative.

evidence.statement: Polymerase II catalyzes DNA-directed RNA synthesis.
The growing RNA 3′ end engages the polymerase active site.
Elongation involves additional factors and can be coupled to RNA processing.
Polymerase II works with other proteins as a molecular complex.
The active site is the region where RNA building blocks are joined.
ATP, UTP, CTP, and GTP are RNA building block precursors used in transcription.
